subject: Food Science
title: Hydrocolloids and Thickeners
description: Learn Hydrocolloids and Thickeners in one minute.

hook.text: Xanthan gum is in your salad dressing, toothpaste, and gluten-free bread. It thickens everything it touches.

buildup.text: Hydrocolloids are large molecules that bind water—creating gels, foams, or thick solutions from tiny amounts.

discovery.text: Agar from seaweed sets firmer than gelatin and stays solid at room temperature. It revolutionized Asian desserts.

twist.text: Some hydrocolloids are shear-thinning—they're thick at rest but flow when squeezed. That's why ketchup pours after a shake.

climax.text: Modernist chefs use hydrocolloids to create caviar from juice, noodles from broth, and foams from anything.

punchline.text: A pinch of powder controls how your food flows, sets, and feels.

quiz.question: Why does ketchup flow after you shake the bottle?
options: Heat from your hand melts it
Its hydrocolloids are shear-thinning—thick at rest, fluid when agitated
